title: "Plant Emotion Detector: Do Plants Detect Human Emotions?"
authorline: "Group 1 — [Full names of all group members]"   # TODO: replace placeholder with real names
studentids: "XXX, XXX, 7380297, 7443682"   # TODO: replace the two XXX with the missing student IDs
supervisor: "Prof. Dr. Peter Gloor"
cosupervisor: "Simon Wolf"
affiliation: "Department of Information Systems for Sustainable Society, Faculty of Management, Economics and Social Sciences, University of Cologne"
runningtitle: "Plant Emotion Detector"
paperabstract: >
  This paper investigates whether a plant's bioelectrical voltage signal
  carries information about the emotional state of a nearby human. In a
  multimodal experiment, 15 participants each watched a fixed sequence of
  emotion-eliciting video clips while a *Kalanchoe* plant's voltage, the
  participant's heart-rate variability (HRV), facial expression, and
  ambient CO~2~ were recorded. Emotion was operationalized along the
  circumplex dimensions of valence (from facial expression via HSEmotion)
  and arousal (from HRV), yielding proxy labels for 284 thirty-second
  windows. Three classifiers --- Random Forest, XGBoost, and a neural
  network --- were trained to predict valence, arousal, and a combined
  emotion label from plant-derived features alone, using
  participant-grouped nested cross-validation and permutation testing.
  The plant signal predicted valence above chance (macro-F1 = 0.42,
  p = 0.005) and the combined label more weakly (p = 0.015), whereas
  arousal did not reach significance (p = 0.055). A partial-correlation
  analysis ruled out ambient CO~2~ as a confounder of the plant--valence
  relationship. The results indicate a weak but statistically robust
  association between plant bioelectrical activity and human valence,
  warranting replication with larger samples and validated ground-truth
  measures.
---
